title: Add the platform's first automated tests (video timing math)
body:
Builds on PR #1 — approve that one first; this stacks on top.

## What this adds

The platform has never had automated tests before — every change has been verified by hand. This PR adds the first ones, focused on the trickiest, most invisible-if-broken part of the video pipeline: the math that decides *when each visual cut happens* relative to the spoken narration.

- **31 automated tests**, all passing.
- They check that the clip timeline always adds up to exactly the length of the narration audio — so a visual never lags behind or cuts off before the voice finishes.
- They check that when the same video clip is reused for multiple cuts, it plays forward through the footage instead of restarting the same few seconds on repeat.
- They check the logic that turns a beat's mood description (e.g. "empty courtroom, cold light") into a safe stock-footage search term, and the logic that detects when a beat is about to show a real person by name (so the pipeline knows not to use a synthetic AI image of them).
- No network calls, no database, no video rendering involved — these are pure math/logic checks, so they run in well under a second and can't flake.

## Why this matters going forward

Right now, if someone accidentally introduced a rounding bug in the timing math, the only way to catch it would be to watch a rendered video and notice the captions or cuts feel "off." These tests catch that kind of bug automatically, the moment it's introduced, before it ever reaches a rendered video.

## What changed under the hood (minimal)

- Added a testing tool (`vitest`) and a `npm test` command.
- Two new test files, nothing else touches how the app behaves.
- One tiny visibility change: a lookup table of footage-source nicknames (like "pexels" → "stock") was made testable directly — no behavior change.

## Verification

- `npm test` → 31/31 passing
- Type-check (`tsc`) → clean, no errors
- No real bugs found in the process — the existing timing math held up under all the edge cases tested (uneven durations, many beats, clip reuse, rounding).

title: Smarter fallback footage: on-theme clips + cleaner upscaling
body:
Builds on PR #1 — approve that one first; this stacks on top.

## What this changes

**1. Fallback footage now matches what the beat is actually about.**
Videos have a "footage ladder" — if there's no AI image, no stock clip, and no archive photo for a moment (say, a courtroom scene), it was supposed to fall back to a generic atmosphere clip from our local mood bank. But the mood bank only had 5 moods (rain, foggy house, police lights, newspaper close-ups, night street) — so a courtroom, prison, forest, highway, water, or interrogation moment had nothing to match and just grabbed a random unrelated clip instead.

Now those 6 themes are recognized too, so those beats reach for something on-theme. A few of the new categories don't have a downloaded clip yet (that needs a one-time `npm run moodbank:populate` run, which searches archive.org for a free, real clip) — until then they gracefully fall back to whatever atmosphere IS available, exactly like before. Nothing is broken by this, it only adds more good matches over time.

**2. Small, blown-up archive clips look intentionally filmic instead of blocky.**
Some of our free archive.org source clips are old and small (think 320×240), and stretching them up to fill a phone screen (1080×1920) made them look pixelated/blocky. Added a light "smooth the grain, then scale up cleanly" step so the same small clip now reads as an intentional vintage/film look instead of a compression mess. Also made the clip-downloader prefer the highest-resolution version when an archive.org item offers more than one file size.

Nothing about how footage is labeled or licensed changed — real-person tagging, AI-generated tagging, and license fields are untouched.

## Test plan
- [x] Type check passes clean (`npx tsc --noEmit`)
- [x] Manually ran the new ffmpeg filter strings against test video clips to confirm they parse and produce the right output size
- [x] Confirmed the manifest JSON is still valid and every new entry is honestly marked as unresolved until a real clip is downloaded

title: Autonomous improvement loop v2 — audit, measure, learn
body:
## What this is

The upgrade to the phone-first improvement loop. The first version could **build**. This one can also **audit, measure, and learn** — which is the difference between agents doing chores and a system that gets better.

## What changed

**Everything moved to GitHub Actions.** The old cloud routines ran on Monday and Sunday and produced *nothing* — no issues, no PRs, and no way to see why from outside. Actions gives us an authenticated `gh`, a readable log for every run, and no 15-runs-per-day cap.

**Three new loops:**

- **Auditor** (`claude-audit.yml`) — every PR gets attacked by an independent agent from five angles (correctness, regression, security, tests, simplicity) *before* you read it. Posts a SHIP / FIX FIRST / DO NOT MERGE verdict.
- **Metrics** (`loop-metrics.yml`) — recomputes `LOOP-DASHBOARD.md` daily from what actually merged. No agent, no tokens. GitHub is the source of truth, not the agents' own self-reports.
- **Retro** (`claude-retro.yml`) — reads what you merged vs. threw away, and proposes fixes to the agents' own instructions via a PR you merge.

**Plus `@claude`** — comment `@claude do X` on any issue or PR from the GitHub mobile app, and an agent picks it up in the cloud. This is the phone remote control.

## How to check it works

1. Merge this.
2. Actions tab → **Claude — Scout** → *Run workflow*. It should file a few `proposal` issues within ~10 minutes.
3. Label one `approved`, then run **Claude — Builder**. It should open a PR, and the auditor should review it automatically.
4. Open `LOOP-DASHBOARD.md` on your phone.

## Risks

- **Needs the `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` secret to exist**, or every Claude workflow fails immediately (loudly, not silently).
- The old cloud routines must be disabled or they'll double-post against these.
- Actions minutes are metered on private repos. The gates keep the nightly builder at ~1 minute when nothing is approved, so this should stay well inside the free tier — worth watching in the first month.

Full owner's manual: `docs/AUTONOMOUS-LOOP.md`.

title: Fix: the loop's agents could not use gh or git (silent no-op)
body:
## What was wrong

The first Scout run finished **green in 6 minutes and filed zero issues** — the exact failure mode that killed the v1 routines.

It was not a reasoning failure. `anthropics/claude-code-action` **disables Bash by default**. The job-level `permissions: issues: write` block grants *GitHub-side* rights, but not *tool-side* ones — so the agent did all four research streams, went to file its proposals, and had every `gh issue create` denied. The only place this surfaces is `permission_denials_count: 20`, buried in the run log.

Every agent workflow had the same hole: Builder could not commit or open a PR, Auditor could not post its verdict, Retro could not open its PR.

## The fix

Adds `--allowedTools` to all five agent workflows:

| Workflow | Allowed |
|---|---|
| Scout, Retro | `Bash(gh:*),Bash(git:*)` |
| Builder, Auditor, @mention | + `Bash(npm:*),Bash(npx:*),Bash(node:*)` (they run tests) |

Also records the failure in `LEARNINGS.md`, with the standing rule: **a green run means "no infra error", not "the task succeeded"** — always verify the outcome on GitHub, and check `permission_denials_count` when output is missing.

All 6 workflow YAMLs parse clean.

title: Make the loop actually run — fix the silent no-op, then run it continuously
body:
## Why the loop produced nothing

Scout ran twice and reported **success** both times. It filed **zero** issues. Zero issues meant nothing for the Builder to build, which is why you never saw more PRs.

Two stacked bugs:

1. The agents were never granted the `Bash` tool, so every `gh issue create` was silently denied — 20 denials, buried in a log nobody reads. The research actually happened; it just couldn't file anything.
2. The first attempt to fix that made it worse. `--allowedTools` **replaces** the toolset rather than adding to it, so granting `Bash(gh:*)` quietly revoked `Read`, `Grep`, `Task` and `WebSearch`. The next run collapsed from 46 turns to 21 — Scout couldn't even research.

Both are fixed here, in all five agent workflows.

## And now it runs continuously

| | Before | Now |
|---|---|---|
| Scout | Mondays 6am | **Every hour** (stands down once 8 proposals are open) |
| Builder | Nightly 3am, only if you'd approved something | **Every 30 min**, picks the best proposal itself |

**The new throttle is your review queue, not the clock.** At most **3 agent PRs** may be waiting on you during the day — merge or close one and the next build starts within 30 minutes. Overnight (11pm–7am ET) the cap lifts so work stacks up while you sleep.

Labelling an issue `approved` still works — it jumps the queue and gets built first. You just don't have to do it anymore for the loop to move.

**You still merge everything.** Agents never push to main.

## Also
- `show_full_output: true` — tool denials are visible in the log instead of hidden.
- Scout now fails loudly if it files nothing, so a green tick can't lie to you again.

title: Fix the real reason nothing gets built: agents quit while their helpers are still working
body:
## What was actually happening

Scout ran, went **green**, and filed **zero issues** — again. This time it was nothing to do with permissions.

Scout spawns four researchers to do its digging. It spawned them **in the background**, then wrote:

> *"I'll wait for their findings to come back... I'll report back with the filed proposals once the researchers return."*

…and ended its turn.

**There is no "later".** A GitHub Actions job is one shot. The moment the agent stops talking, the container is destroyed. The four researchers were killed mid-flight and the step that actually files the issues was never reached. It even ran `sleep 1; echo "checking..."` as filler while it "waited".

The run reported `stop_reason: end_turn`, zero errors, zero permission denials. **A perfectly green run that produced nothing.**

## The fix

The Builder (3 helpers) and Auditor (5 helpers) use the identical pattern, so all three had this bug. Each now gets an explicit brief up front: there is no second turn, helpers must be run in the foreground, and **the job is not done until the issue / PR / comment actually exists on GitHub.**

## And a check that can't lie

The Scout verify step *did* catch this — "0 proposals before → 0 after" — but only logged a **warning**, so the run stayed green and you spent a day thinking the loop was working.

It now **fails the run**. A red X is information. A green tick that did nothing is a lie.

title: Reliability: stop marking broken or silent videos as "done"
body:
## The problem (in plain terms)
When a video fails to actually render — or ends up with **no voiceover** — the app currently marks the run as **completed / approved anyway**, and for hands-off ("auto") agents it will even try to **publish** it. The dashboard shows green, but there's no real video, or a silent one.

This is the single worst experience for a non-technical owner: the system *lies* about success. It's also the exact failure the loop's own `LEARNINGS.md` warns about ("a green run that did nothing is a lie") — just at the video level instead of the CI level.

## Evidence (verified in this repo)
- `src/lib/truecrime/assemble.ts:293-296` — `assembleVideo()` **returns** `{ outputPath: null, rendered: false }` when ffmpeg is missing or `final.mp4` isn't produced. It does **not** throw.
- `src/lib/truecrime/orchestrator.ts:212-233` — the `assemble` stage never checks `ctx.render.rendered`; it writes `localPath: outputPath ?? undefined`, then proceeds to `finalStatus = 'approved'` and `maybeAutoPublish(...)`. Same pattern in `src/lib/history/orchestrator.ts`.
- Contrast: the **sports** pipeline does it right — `src/lib/tools/assemble.ts:84` throws `'ffmpeg finished but final.mp4 not found'`. The two most-used factories are the ones that swallow it.
- Silent audio: `src/lib/truecrime/tts.ts:286-289` falls back to a `silent-stub` (flat silent track) when every TTS provider fails, and nothing downstream inspects `provider` — so a voiceless video renders, gets `approved`, and can auto-publish.

## What to build
1. In both narrated orchestrators' `assemble` stage: if `!ctx.render.outputPath || !ctx.render.rendered`, **throw** so the stage retries and, if it still fails, the run is marked **failed** with a visible reason (mirror the sports pipeline).
2. Treat a `silent-stub` TTS result as a soft failure: force the video to `status='review'` (never auto-publish) and record a plain-English reason ("no voiceover was produced").

## Effort
**S–M** — small, surgical changes in 2-3 files; no schema change required.

## How we'd know it worked
Run a factory with ffmpeg's renderer disabled (or TTS unreachable): the run ends as **failed / needs-review with a clear reason**, and **no** empty or silent video ever reaches `approved` or gets published.

title: Tell the owner WHY an auto-post didn't happen (instead of silently stopping)
body:
## The problem (in plain terms)
When a hands-off ("auto") agent finishes a video but **can't publish it** — YouTube isn't connected, the daily quota is used up, or the upload is rejected — the app quietly leaves the video sitting in "approved" and says nothing. The owner just notices "my channel stopped posting" days later, with no clue why.

## Evidence (verified in this repo)
- `src/lib/tools/publish.ts:197-203` — `maybeAutoPublish()` catches every failure and returns it as a `reason` string instead of throwing.
- But the callers **throw that return value away**: `src/lib/truecrime/orchestrator.ts:247`, `src/lib/history/orchestrator.ts` (~:254), and `src/lib/orchestrator.ts` (~:154) all call `maybeAutoPublish(...)` without using the result.
- Net effect: "quota reached", "YouTube not connected", or an upload 403 leaves the video `approved` with the reason surfaced **nowhere**.

## What to build
- Persist the auto-publish outcome so it shows up in the UI — e.g. write a `Post` row with `status='failed'` + reason, or store the reason on the `AgentRun`.
- Surface it in the Review inbox / run view in plain language ("Not posted: YouTube daily limit reached — will retry tomorrow").

## Effort
**S–M** — mostly wiring an already-produced reason string into a stored field + one UI badge.

## How we'd know it worked
Disconnect YouTube (or exhaust the quota) and run an auto agent: the video shows a clear **"not posted, here's why"** message in the dashboard instead of silently sitting in "approved".

title: Recover runs that get stuck "running" forever after a crash or restart
body:
## The problem (in plain terms)
Runs execute inside the web app itself, with no background daemon. If the dev server reloads (which happens on any file save), crashes, or runs out of memory mid-render, the run is left marked **"running" forever** and the video **"rendering" forever**. Nothing ever reconciles them. The owner sees a run stuck spinning with no error and no way to tell it's actually dead.

## Evidence (verified in this repo)
- `src/app/api/agents/[id]/run/route.ts:9-12` — runs are fire-and-forget (`.catch(console.error)`); a crash between start and finish never updates status.
- The orchestrators only move a run out of `running` inside their own `try/catch`, so an interrupted process leaves `AgentRun.status='running'` and `Video.status='rendering'` permanently.

## What to build
- On app startup (and/or inside the scheduler `tick`), find runs stuck in `running` past a sane timeout and mark them **failed** with reason "interrupted (app restarted mid-run)". Reset their videos out of `rendering`.
- Optionally surface a "this run was interrupted — re-run?" action in the UI.

## Effort
**S** — a single reconciliation pass keyed on `updatedAt` age; no schema change.

## How we'd know it worked
Kill the server mid-render, restart it: the stuck run flips to **failed/interrupted** within one tick instead of spinning forever, and the owner can re-run it.

title: Protect the channel from demonetization: extend the anti-repetition gate to every factory
body:
## The problem (in plain terms)
YouTube's 2025–2026 "inauthentic / mass-produced content" crackdown is the biggest existential risk to a faceless-automation channel. The platform now demonetizes — and has **terminated** — channels whose videos are repetitive and template-identical. One enforcement wave wiped 16 channels (~4.7B lifetime views, 35M subscribers); one creator reported losing $250K/month overnight.
- Evidence: https://www.bottlerocketcontent.com/youtube-ai-slop-crackdown-faceless-creators-2026/ (quotes YouTube's own policy wording), and creators report the algorithm throttles reach after just 5–7 near-identical uploads: https://easyviral.ai/blog/youtube-shorts-getting-0-views-7-fixes-2026

## The good news: we already own the fix — for one factory only
This repo already ships a real anti-repetition system: `checkVariation()` in `src/lib/compliance/variation.ts` (hook-pattern + section-sequence + narration-shingle similarity, routes to human review over a threshold) plus footage de-dup in `src/lib/compliance/visualSignature.ts`. **But it's wired into the True Crime pipeline only.** The Reddit, Sports, and History factories mass-produce with **no** template-similarity brake.

## What to build
- Extend the existing variation + visual-signature gate to run for **every** factory before a video is approved/published, comparing each new video's hook, structure, voice, music bed, and footage set against that agent's recent uploads.
- When overlap crosses the threshold, route to review (or auto-vary hook/template/voice) instead of publishing another near-duplicate.
- Maintain small rotating pools (hook templates, intros, music beds, voices) so variation is automatic.

## Effort
**M** — mostly generalizing already-tested code (`variation.ts` has coverage) from one orchestrator to the shared path.

## How we'd know it worked
Generate 10 videos from the same factory back-to-back: the gate flags/forces variation on the near-duplicates instead of letting a wall of identical uploads go out.

title: Give every video a strong hook — and learn which hooks actually win
body:
## The problem (in plain terms)
On Shorts/Reels/TikTok the first 1–3 seconds decide everything — roughly 50–60% of viewers drop off there, and you need very high average-view-% to get real distribution. "Most failed AI faceless videos are dead before the first scene is rendered." Weak hooks = 0 views = 0 revenue, no matter how good the rest is.

1. **Hook gate in the script stage** (`src/lib/tools/script.ts` and the true-crime/history script builders): have Claude generate 3–5 candidate opening lines, score them (curiosity / specificity / pattern-interrupt), and pick the strongest. Store the chosen hook + score.
2. **Close the loop with analytics we already pull.** `src/lib/tools/analytics.ts` already retrieves average-view-% / watch time. ## Effort
**M** — one extra Claude call in the script stage + a scoring/feedback table joined to existing metrics.

## How we'd know it worked
Every new video stores a hook score; after ~20 published videos the agent measurably favors the hook styles with the highest real retention, and low-retention templates stop being reused.

title: Stop the sports channel from getting killed by copyright strikes
body:
## The problem in one line
Our **sports factory downloads real broadcast highlight reels off YouTube and re-uploads a cropped version with no copyright check at all** — which is the single most common way faceless sports channels get terminated.

## What's actually happening in our code
- `src/lib/tools/clipIngest.ts` pulls the source highlight reel straight from YouTube via `yt-dlp`, keeps a ~20s window, and we render/publish a vertical crop of it.
- There is **no license or copyright gate anywhere in the sports pipeline.** The footage goes from "someone else's copyrighted broadcast" to "published on our channel" untouched by any check.
- We already built exactly this kind of gate for the **true-crime** side: `src/lib/compliance/visualLint.ts` refuses to ship any asset whose license is `unknown` and requires a logged license reference. The sports factory simply never calls it. The plumbing (`AssetLicense` types in `src/lib/compliance/types.ts`, the lint itself) already exists — it's just not wired in for sports.

## Why this matters to the channel's survival
This isn't a "claim splits your revenue" nuisance — leagues issue real **DMCA strikes**, and **3 strikes in 90 days = the whole channel is permanently deleted.** Sports is the worst-exposed niche there is.

Evidence:
- "Sports leagues actively patrol YouTube and issue DMCA takedowns (strikes), not just Content ID claims... even 10-second clips [trigger] immediate strikes from NFL, NBA, Premier League." — https://subscribr.ai/p/avoid-youtube-strikes-ai-faceless-channel
- Faceless channels "expose 60–80% of video content to copyright scanning... receiving 6–8x more Content ID claims." — https://virvid.ai/blog/youtube-copyright-mistakes-faceless-creators-2026
- On **July 15, 2025 YouTube tightened its monetization rules** against "inauthentic" reused/compilation content that doesn't add clear transformation. Background music alone "triggers more copyright claims than all other content combined." — https://onewrk.com/youtube-copyright-claim-complete-guide-2025/

Two separate research angles (user pain + revenue risk) independently ranked this the **#1 existential threat** to this product.

## What to build
1. Wire the existing `visualLint`/license model into the **sports** assemble path so a clip with no accounted-for license can't be published (fail closed, matching the true-crime side).
2. A **pre-publish copyright-risk gate** that flags high-risk sources (known-league broadcast footage, unlicensed background music) and requires a "transformation checklist" to pass — voiceover added, reframed to 9:16, zoom/overlay graphics applied, clip kept short — so we lean on transformative use instead of raw re-upload.
3. Surface the risk verdict in the owner's review inbox so a high-risk video is flagged *before* it goes out, not after a strike lands.

## Effort
**M** — the license model and lint already exist for true crime; this is mostly wiring them into the sports pipeline plus the risk heuristics/checklist. (True Content-ID matching can't run locally, so this is rules-based + leaning on YouTube's own pre-publish Checks.)

## How we'd know it worked
No sports video can reach `published` while carrying an unaccounted-for/unlicensed source clip, and every high-risk video is flagged in the review inbox before publishing.

title: Stop marking broken or silent videos as "done" (#14)
body:
Closes #14

## What changed
Two of your video pipelines — **True Crime** and **History** — had a hidden honesty bug. They could finish a run, mark the video **approved**, and even **auto-post it**, in two cases where there was nothing good to post:

1. **The video file never actually got made** (the renderer/ffmpeg wasn't available, or the final file was missing).
2. **The video came out silent** — every voice provider failed, so it fell back to a muted track with no narration.

Now the app is honest about both:

- **No video file** → the run **stops and shows as Failed** with a clear reason, instead of pretending it succeeded. (Your Sports pipeline already did this — the other two just weren't.)
- **Silent video** → it's **held in your Review inbox and never auto-posted**, with a plain-English note in the Queue saying *"No voiceover was produced…"*.

The decision logic lives in one small shared file with automated tests, so both pipelines stay in sync and this can't silently regress.

## Why it matters
Right now the dashboard can show green — "done", even "posted" — when there's actually no real video, or a silent one. For a hands-off channel that's the worst kind of failure: you'd only notice much later, after a blank or silent clip went public. This makes the system tell the truth instead.

## How to check it works (click by click)
You don't have to break anything to trust it — the automated tests cover the logic. But if you want to see it live:

1. Run an **auto** agent in a setup where video rendering can't complete (e.g. ffmpeg unavailable).
2. Open the dashboard **Queue** tab. Instead of a green "done", you'll see that run marked **Failed** with the reason *"Assemble finished but produced no video file…"*.
3. For the silent case: if voice generation fails, the video lands in the **Review inbox** (not posted), and the Queue shows a red **voiceover** step: *"No voiceover was produced…"*.

- **Low risk.** The change is small (one new tested helper file + a guard in each of the two orchestrators) and mirrors behaviour the Sports pipeline already uses.
- Possible side effect: in an environment where rendering genuinely can't run, those runs will now show as **Failed** instead of silently "succeeding". That's the intended fix, but it means you may see honest failures where before you saw fake successes.

title: Recover runs stuck "running" forever after a crash or restart
body:
Closes #16

## What changed
Runs are executed **inside the web app** with no background worker. So if the dev server reloads (which happens on **any file save**), crashes, or runs out of memory in the middle of making a video, the run was left stuck on **"running"** and the video stuck on **"rendering"** — forever, with no error. A spinner that never stops.

This adds a small clean-up pass. Whenever the scheduler ticks, the app now looks for work left over from a crash and marks it **Failed** with a plain-English reason: *"Interrupted — the app crashed or restarted while this run was in progress."* You can then just re-run it.

It only cleans up work that's been stuck for **30 minutes**, so a genuinely long render is never cut off by mistake. (You can change that with a `RUN_STUCK_TIMEOUT_MIN` setting, but you don't need to.)

## Why it matters
Today a crash mid-render leaves the dashboard showing a video that spins forever, with nothing telling you it's actually dead — you'd only notice "my videos stopped" days later. Now the stuck item turns into a clear **Failed** you can see and re-run.

## How to check it works (click by click)
1. Start the app: `npm run go`, open http://localhost:3000
2. Kick off a run (an agent's **Run** button) so a video starts **rendering**.
3. Kill the server mid-render: in a terminal run `lsof -ti:3000 | xargs kill`
4. Restart it: `npm run go`
5. Within about a minute, that stuck item flips from a spinning **"Rendering"** to a red **"Failed"** badge on the dashboard's Recent Activity — instead of spinning forever. The server log prints a `[recovery] reset …` line too.

(There's also an automated test covering the 30-minute timeout logic; `npm test` stays green.)

## What could break
- **Very low risk.** The clean-up only touches work older than 30 minutes that's still marked in-progress, so it can't interrupt a live run. And if it ever did flag one too early, that self-corrects: when the real render finishes it overwrites the row with its true status.
- No database schema changes. One new small file (`src/lib/recovery.ts`) plus a few lines in the scheduler; nothing else changed.

## Deliberately left small (possible follow-ups)
- A one-click **"Re-run"** button on interrupted runs.
- Cleaning up videos stuck at **"queued"** (from a crash *before* rendering even starts) — this PR handles the "rendering" case the issue asked for.

title: Your spending cap doesn't actually stop spending — make the budget limit real
body:
## The problem in one line
The app **promises to stop spending your money at a limit you set — but that limit does nothing.** The "budget cap" and "monthly ceiling" boxes are collected, saved, and then read by no part of the system.

## What's actually happening in our code
- When you create an agent, the form says, word for word: *"Orchestrator will abort the run if Claude + media costs exceed this amount."* (`src/app/agents/new/page.tsx:285`)
- Settings says: *"Alerts when monthly spend approaches the ceiling."* (`src/app/settings/page.tsx:197`)
- Both values are stored (`budget` on the agent in `prisma/schema.prisma:39`; `monthly_budget` in Settings).
- **But no code ever reads them.** A repo-wide search for any budget check in the engine (`src/lib/**`) returns **zero** results — the orchestrator that runs a factory (`src/lib/orchestrator.ts`) never looks at `agent.budget`, and nothing anywhere reads `monthly_budget`. There is no abort, no alert, no counter.

## Why this matters to the owner
Every video spends real money — paid TTS, image generation, and Claude calls. A factory that gets stuck in a retry loop, or an over-eager overnight batch, can bill **unbounded** with no brake and no warning. The owner is a non-technical operator who set a cap *specifically so this couldn't happen* — and the interface told him it was handled. That is the worst kind of gap: a safety control that looks real and isn't. It is also a straightforward trust problem — the UI states a guarantee the code doesn't keep.

## Evidence
- UI promise: `src/app/agents/new/page.tsx:285` and `src/app/settings/page.tsx:197`
- Field exists but is never consumed: `budget Float?` at `prisma/schema.prisma:39`; grep for `budget` / `monthly_budget` across `src/lib` finds no reader.
- The cost data needed to enforce it **already exists** — the per-run cost is already summed today (e.g. `src/lib/truecrime/orchestrator.ts` rolls Claude + media spend into a per-video figure), so the enforcement just needs to compare that running total against the cap.

## What to build
1. **Per-run hard stop:** before/while a factory run spends, track the running cost and abort the run (mark it failed with a clear reason) the moment it would exceed the agent's `budget`. Make the promise on the button true.
2. **Monthly ceiling alert:** sum this month's spend from the cost ledger and, when it nears/crosses `monthly_budget`, surface a plain-language warning in the dashboard (and stop auto-runs if over).
3. If we decide *not* to build enforcement now, at minimum change the UI text so it stops promising a guarantee that doesn't exist.

## Effort
**S–M** — the cost is already being tallied per run; this is a comparison + an abort path + one dashboard warning. Monthly rollup is the M part.

## How we'd know it worked
Set an agent's budget to a tiny number and start a run: it stops itself and shows *"Stopped: run hit your $X budget cap"* instead of billing past it. Set a low monthly ceiling and the dashboard warns as spend approaches it.

When a hands-off ("auto") agent makes a video but **can't post it to YouTube**, the app used to leave it sitting in "Approved" and say nothing — you'd only notice days later that the channel had gone quiet. Now the dashboard tells you **why** in plain English, right on the front page.

title: Videos still get stuck on "Queued" forever — the crash-recovery fix only covers the last step
body:
## The problem in one line
The crash-recovery you just approved only rescues videos that died at the **very last** step — so a video that crashes at any earlier step still gets stuck showing **"Queued" forever**, with no error and no way to notice.

## Why this matters (plain terms)
Last week we shipped the fix that stops runs from spinning forever after a crash or restart (PR #25). It works — but only partway. A video goes through many steps (finding a source, writing the script, gathering footage, voiceover, compliance checks) and **only reaches the "rendering" step at the very end**. The recovery sweep only looks for videos stuck at that final "rendering" step. So if the app crashes or reloads during any of the earlier steps — which is where the video spends **almost all** of its time — that video is left frozen as **"Queued"** on your dashboard. The run and its job get correctly marked "failed," but the video itself is orphaned: it shows a blue "Queued" badge indefinitely, never lands in your review Inbox, and never shows as Failed. It's the exact "permanent spinner with no error" the recovery module was written to eliminate — just one stage short of covering it.

## Evidence (verified in this repo)
- Recovery only sweeps `rendering`: `src/lib/recovery.ts:67-70` — `Video.updateMany({ where: { status: 'rendering', ... } })`.
- But every video is **created as `queued`**: `src/lib/orchestrator.ts:31`, `src/lib/truecrime/orchestrator.ts:45`, `src/lib/history/orchestrator.ts:52`.
- And only flips to `rendering` at the **final assemble step**: `src/lib/orchestrator.ts:133`, `src/lib/truecrime/orchestrator.ts:220`, `src/lib/history/orchestrator.ts:227`.
- The module's own docstring says its whole job is to end "a spinner that never stops and no error" (`src/lib/recovery.ts:6-8`) — the current sweep just misses the stages where crashes are most likely.
- **Secondary gap:** recovery only matches `Job.status === 'running'`, but the orchestrator marks jobs `retrying` during backoff (`src/lib/orchestrator.ts` retry path), so a job orphaned mid-retry is also never healed.

## What to build
- Extend `recoverStuckRuns` so a stuck **`queued`** video (older than the timeout, and whose run was just marked failed) is also flipped to `failed` with the interrupted reason — so it surfaces as Failed / in the Inbox instead of a frozen "Queued" badge.
- Include `retrying` jobs in the same sweep so a job orphaned mid-backoff is healed too.
- Reuse the existing timeout guard so a genuinely-live queued video is never killed.

## Effort

title: A dead YouTube login still shows "Connected" — so posting silently stops and nothing warns you
body:
## The problem in one line
When your YouTube login quietly expires, the app **keeps showing a green "Connected"** — while every auto-publish silently fails, so videos stop posting and nothing tells you why.

## Why this matters (plain terms)
Google refresh tokens expire on their own: a password change, a security reset, revoking access, or ~6 months of the app sitting idle all silently invalidate the connection. When that happens, the Settings page **still says "Connected as [your channel]"** because the app only ever checks whether a connection row is marked "active" — and the only thing that ever un-marks it is you clicking **Disconnect** by hand. So the connection dies, but the light stays green. Every scheduled video then tries to publish, fails deep inside the YouTube call, gets quietly logged as a failed post, and the run still reports "success." You'd see videos silently stop reaching YouTube with a dashboard insisting everything's fine — the same "it stopped and didn't tell me" pain we just fixed for the "why didn't a video post" case (PR #28/#29), but one level up: the *connection itself* is lying about its health.

## Evidence (verified in this repo)
- Connection is judged healthy purely by an "active" flag: `src/lib/youtube.ts:107` — `where: { platform: PLATFORM, status: 'active' }`.
- The Settings UI paints "Connected as X" straight off that (`src/app/settings/page.tsx` connection status).
- The **only** thing that ever sets a non-active status is the manual Disconnect button (`src/app/api/auth/youtube/route.ts`). A real Google `invalid_grant` never flips it.
- When the token is dead, `authedClient()` throws inside googleapis on every call (`src/lib/youtube.ts:104-138`); the auto-publish path swallows it into a failed Post and the run still completes.
- Compounding it: the rotated-token save in `authedClient` is fire-and-forget (`void (async () => …)()`) with no error handling, so a failed token write is silent too.

## What to build
1. **Detect the dead connection:** when a publish/refresh call fails with an auth error (`invalid_grant` / 401), flip the connection's status (e.g. to `needs_reconnect`) instead of leaving it "active."
2. **Tell the owner, plainly:** Settings (and ideally the dashboard) shows "**YouTube disconnected — reconnect to resume publishing**" with the reconnect button, instead of a false green light.
3. Optional: a lightweight health check so the status reflects reality without waiting for the next scheduled post to fail.

## Effort
**S–M** — catch the auth error on the existing publish path, update one status field, and change the Settings copy/CTA. No new pipeline stages.

## How we'd know it worked
Revoke the app's access in your Google account, then trigger a publish: Settings switches to "Disconnected — reconnect" and the dashboard flags it, instead of continuing to show "Connected" while posts silently fail.

title: Fix the loop: approving an issue now starts a build immediately
body:
## What changed

Three fixes to the Builder, all from problems we hit today.

**1. Approving an issue now starts a build within a minute.**
Before: approving only did something when the 30-minute timer happened to fire — and GitHub keeps *dropping* those timers. Today it fired at 14:02, then not again until 15:59. You approved three issues and nothing happened for an hour. Now the Builder wakes up the moment you tick `approved`.

**2. The Builder can no longer build the same thing twice.**
It built issue #15 twice today — PRs #28 and #29 — and you had to throw one away. It was supposed to prevent that by commenting "I've started this" on the issue, but nothing ever *read* that comment. Now the check happens before the agent starts: any issue that already has an open PR is off limits.

**3. The Builder now reads your comments on an issue.**
Before, it only read the issue's description. So if you commented "only do the YouTube part," it never saw it and built the original thing anyway. Now it reads the whole thread and treats your comments as overriding the description. And when you ask `@claude` to change an issue's scope, it edits the description to match.

## Why it matters

The loop was quietly wasting runs and ignoring you. This is what made "I approved it and nothing happened" happen.

## How to check it works

1. Merge this.
2. On your phone, label any proposal `approved`.
3. Open the repo's **Actions** tab — a **Builder** run should appear within about a minute (before, you'd wait up to an hour, sometimes longer).
4. ~12 minutes later a PR shows up, assigned to you.

## What could break

The Builder now runs on label events as well as the timer. The `if:` guard means it only wakes for the `approved` label, and the existing queue cap (3 open PRs daytime) still stops it running away. Worst case it's a no-op run that costs ~15 seconds.

title: Stop the sports channel from getting killed by copyright strikes (#21)
body:
## What changed
Every **sports video** now goes through a **copyright safety check** the moment it's finished — *before* it can ever post. If a clip looks risky, it's **held in your Review inbox** with a plain-English explanation instead of going out.

The check does three things:
- **Fails closed.** Our sports clips are downloaded from someone else's broadcast with no license on file — so by default **every one now waits for your approval** instead of auto-posting. This is the single biggest way faceless sports channels get deleted by copyright strikes.
- **Grades how "transformed" the clip is** — did we add our own commentary, reframe it to vertical, add zoom/graphics, keep it short? A plain cropped re-upload fails and gets flagged.
- **Flags the danger signs** — strike-happy leagues (NFL, UFC) and borrowed background music are marked **high risk**.

Your **Review inbox now shows the verdict** on each sports card with simple colored chips: *Copyright review needed*, *Copyright risk: High/Medium/Low*, and whether the *transformation checklist passed* — so a risky video is caught **before** a strike can land.

## Why it matters
Until now **nothing ever checked the finished sports video** — a copyrighted broadcast clip could walk straight to publish. Three strikes in 90 days deletes the whole channel. This puts a fail-closed gate in the way and reuses the exact same safety plumbing already trusted on the True Crime side, so it's consistent.

## How to check it works (click by click)
1. Start the app: `npm run go`, then open the **Agents** page.
2. Find **Sports Highlights Agent** and click **Run** (it downloads + builds a clip in the background — give it a few minutes).
3. Open the **Review Inbox** tab. When the run finishes, an **F9** sports card appears.
4. On that card, look at the **review reasons** — you'll now see the new copyright chips, e.g. a yellow **"Copyright review needed"**, a red **"Copyright risk: High"** (because the source clip has no logged license), and a green **"Transformation checklist passed"** with **"4/4 transform steps"** — plus a one-line plain-English summary.
5. Approve or reject as normal. Nothing auto-posts while it's sitting here.

> Note: with the demo setup you'll normally see the yellow **"review needed"** state (held for you), not a red **"Blocked"** one — blocking only happens if you configure a league as fully off-limits. To let a clean clip auto-post later, log a real source license in the factory config on a tolerant league (e.g. NBA) with the transform edits on.

- **Nothing auto-posts for sports anymore by default** — this is intentional (fail-closed), but it means the Sports agent won't publish on its own until you either approve items or log a license. Say the word if you'd rather a specific factory be allowed to auto-post.
- This is smart rules + a fail-closed gate — **it can't run YouTube's real copyright scanner locally** (nobody outside YouTube can), so it slashes strike risk but can't promise zero.

Your original ask was for an evaluation loop that *actually watches the frames* of each video with AI, plus a "golden set" to keep it honest over time. This PR ships the **per-video gate you endorsed ("build it out")** — the core of the issue — using smart rules. The two next steps, exactly as researched:

title: Make the budget cap actually stop a run (#26)
body:
## What changed
The app has always had a **budget cap** box when you create an agent, with the promise: *"Orchestrator will abort the run if Claude + media costs exceed this amount."* That promise was **empty** — the number was saved but no part of the system ever looked at it, so a run could bill past your cap with no brake.

This PR makes the cap **real**. Before each step of making a video, the system now adds up what this run has already spent and, the moment that reaches your cap, it **stops the run** instead of spending more. The stopped run is marked failed with a plain message: **"Stopped: run hit your $X budget cap."**

You'll see that message in two places:
- On the **home/Overview screen** under the video in Recent Activity (no clicking needed).
- On the **Queue** tab, on the step where it stopped.

If you leave the cap blank (or 0), nothing changes — runs behave exactly as they do today.

## Why it matters
Every video spends real money (paid voice, image generation, Claude). A factory stuck in a retry loop or an over-eager overnight batch could otherwise run up an **unbounded** bill. You set a cap specifically so that couldn't happen — now it can't. It also fixes a trust gap: the screen was stating a guarantee the code didn't keep.

## How to check it works (click by click)
1. Go to **Agents → New Agent**.
2. Pick any factory and set **Budget cap per run** to a *tiny* number — use **`0.001`** (one tenth of a cent). It has to be smaller than one real run costs, or the cap will never be reached and the run just finishes normally.
3. Create the agent, then press **Run** on its card.
4. Open the **home/Overview** screen (or the **Queue** tab). Within a few steps the run flips to **Failed** with **"Stopped: run hit your $0.001 budget cap"** — instead of quietly billing past it.
5. Now make another agent with the cap left **blank** and run it: it completes as normal. (Proves we didn't change anything for agents without a cap.)

## What could break
- **The stop happens *between* steps, not mid-step.** The system can't un-spend a call that's already running, so the one step that crosses the line finishes; every step after it is blocked. Real spend can therefore land slightly over the cap (by roughly one step's cost), never far past it. This is the honest, safe behaviour.
- Agents **without** a cap are untouched (the check is skipped entirely — no extra work, no behaviour change).
- Applies to all three video types (sports, true crime, history) through the shared step-runner they all use.

## Deliberately left out (kept this small on purpose)
The issue also asked for a **monthly spending ceiling** with a dashboard warning (item 2, the bigger piece). That's a good follow-up; this PR does the headline **per-run hard stop** only, so it's easy to review and hard to get wrong.

## Tests
Added unit tests for the budget logic. Full suite passes (197 passed) and the production build is green.

Closes #26

## The one-line version

Right now the app **can see** which videos win, but it **never uses that** to decide what to make next. It picks topics off a fixed rotation and ignores your analytics entirely. This proposal wires up the "learn from winners" loop — the single feature the whole product was pitched on.

- **PRD goal #5 (`docs/PRD.md`):** *"Closed feedback loop. Use analytics to inform what to make next (which formats/topics/hooks win → feed the ideation step)"* — described as *"the real proof the system works."*
- **`docs/Decision-and-Cost-Guide.md`:** *"the analytics feedback loop… is the most important revenue feature in the whole product."*

In plain terms: the pitch was *"double down on what works, cut what doesn't."* Today the system does neither. It generates on autopilot forever regardless of what actually earns views — which means real API money keeps flowing into formats and topics that flop.

## The proof it's genuinely missing (verified in code)

- **Topics are chosen by the calendar, not by performance.** Every factory picks its next subject with `new Date().getDate() % watchlist.length` — a day-of-month rotation (`src/lib/tools/source.ts:68` & `:85` for sports; `src/lib/truecrime/caseDiscovery.ts:251` for true-crime/history). 1. After metrics refresh, rank each agent's recent videos by views (and watch-% once available) and write a short plain-text "what's winning" digest into that agent's existing `Agent.memory` field — e.g. *"Top performers: [topic A], [topic B]; best hooks: [style]. Weakest: [topic C]."*
2. At the start of each run, read that digest and feed it into the topic-picking / script stage so the agent **biases toward proven topics and hooks and away from duds**, instead of blind calendar rotation.
3. Show the digest on the dashboard so you can see *why* it chose what it chose.

This uses data already in the database and a field that already exists — it's wiring, not new infrastructure.

**M** — scoped to the first version above. (Full "one-click clone a winner" and cross-factory learning can follow as separate, smaller steps.)

## How we'd know it worked

Videos made **after** a winner-digest exists beat the pre-loop baseline on median views per factory — which is the PRD's own stated success test ("do 'make more like this' videos outperform baseline?"). Minimum bar for v1: each agent's `memory` field visibly fills with a real winners summary, and the next run's chosen topic can be traced back to it.

title: Stop an auto-posted true-crime video from calling a real, living person guilty — the legal safety check has holes and zero tests
body:
## The risk in plain English

Your true-crime factory can run on autopilot: it writes a script, narrates it, renders it, and posts it — no human in the loop when an agent is set to fully-automatic. The one thing standing between that pipeline and a **defamation lawsuit** is a single safety check that reads the narration and blocks any sentence that flatly states a *living, not-convicted* real person committed the crime.

That check has two problems, and right now **nothing tests it at all**, so a future change could quietly break it and no alarm would go off.

## What's actually wrong

**1. It only catches a name if the script writes it exactly the way it's stored.**
The guard skips any sentence unless the person's *full stored name* appears as a literal substring:

- `src/lib/compliance/defamationLint.ts:59` — `if (!sentence.toLowerCase().includes(subj.name.toLowerCase())) continue`

So if the case subject is stored as **\"John Smith\"** but the narration says **\"Smith pulled the trigger\"** or **\"John did it\"**, the sentence is never checked → the gate returns **pass** → an auto agent can publish it. Worse: if the AI script names a person who **isn't in the case's subject list at all** (easy to happen — the LLM adds a boyfriend, a neighbor, a suspect), that name is invisible to the guard and gets zero protection.

**2. The entire legal-safety module has no tests.**
Confirmed: `find src/lib/compliance -name '*.test.ts'` returns nothing. The decision engine (`gate.ts`) and every check it calls (`defamationLint.ts`, `corroboration.ts`, `legalStatus.ts`, `claims.ts`, `caseSelection.ts`) are untested. This is the highest-stakes code in the repo — the part that keeps you out of court — and it's the least protected. A refactor or a change in the AI's output shape could disable it silently, with a green build and no failing test.

## What to build

- Tighten name matching in `defamationLint.ts` so it also catches **last-name-only / first-name-only / alias** mentions of a stored subject.
- Treat **\"a person is named in the narration with a guilt verb but isn't in the subject list\"** as an automatic **route-to-review** (don't auto-publish), instead of silently passing.
- Add a real unit-test suite around `gate.ts` and `defamationLint.ts` covering: full name, partial name, unknown name, convicted vs. living-unconvicted, hedged vs. unhedged — so this protection can never be broken without a test going red.

## Evidence
- `src/lib/compliance/defamationLint.ts:59` (substring-only match) and `:67` (living + no-hedge → `block`)
- `src/lib/compliance/gate.ts` header: \"block → do not produce … defamation 'block' flag … lands here\" — this is the sole gate on autonomous true-crime output
- `src/lib/compliance/` has **no** `*.test.ts` files (verified)
- Category context — 2026 platform + legal pressure on faceless true-crime naming real people: https://virvid.ai/blog/youtube-copyright-mistakes-faceless-creators-2026

## Effort
**M** — mostly test-writing plus a tightening of the name-matching and one new review trigger. No schema or UI change required.

## How we'd know it worked
A test suite exists for the compliance gate, and a script that says **\"Smith killed her\"** (subject stored as \"John Smith\", living, not convicted) — or names a person not in the subject list at all — is held for review instead of auto-published.

title: The AI voice mispronounces names, places & acronyms — add a pronunciation step before every voiceover
body:
## The problem in one line
The AI voice reads your scripts as-is, so it **mispronounces exactly the words your niches are built on** — athlete and team names, victims' and criminals' names, historical figures, places, acronyms (it says "fibby" for FBI), and numbers/dates — and one butchered name in the first few seconds makes a video sound careless and kills trust in the comments.

## Why this matters to the product's success
- All four of your factories are **dense with proper nouns**: Sports (players, teams), True Crime (names, places), History (figures, dates), Reddit (names, brands). These are precisely the words neural TTS gets wrong most often — and precisely the words that carry the story.
- Wrong pronunciations are one of the most-cited complaints about faceless AI videos, because viewers instantly read them as "no human checked this." That's both a credibility problem and part of the "AI slop" signal platforms are now penalising.
- It compounds the feedback you already gave — that the videos felt flat/low-effort. Getting names right is one of the cheapest ways to sound like a real channel.
- Evidence this is a known, structural TTS problem (not solvable by "pick a better voice"): https://www.planetlanguages.com/ai-voiceover-problems/ and ElevenLabs' own guidance on pronunciation dictionaries: https://help.elevenlabs.io/hc/en-us/articles/19448694780177

title: Stop the voice mispronouncing names & acronyms — add a pronunciation step before every voiceover
body:
Closes #51

## What changed (plain English)
Right now the AI voice reads your scripts exactly as written, so it butchers the
words your channels are built on — it says **"fibby" for FBI**, trips over tricky
names, and reads years like a phone number. One mangled name in the first few
seconds makes a video sound like nobody checked it.

This adds a small **"say it right" step** that runs on the narration **just before
the voice records it**, for both your **True Crime** and **History** videos:

- **Acronyms** get spelled out so they're read letter-by-letter — "FBI" is now
  spoken **"F B I"** (but see below: on screen it still *reads* "FBI").
- **Years and decades** are read the natural way — "1995" → **"nineteen
  ninety-five"**, "the 1980s" → **"the nineteen eighties"**.
- **Tricky names** are corrected from a built-in list (e.g. Gaddafi, Dahmer,
  Versailles, Worcester, Qatar). You can add your own over time — see below.

**The captions still look right.** This was the tricky part: normally, fixing the
audio would also make the on-screen captions say "F B I" or a phonetic respelling.
The code now keeps the *original spelling* for the captions while the *voice* gets
the corrected version. So your viewers **hear it right and read it right.**

## Why it matters
- Getting names right is one of the cheapest ways to stop videos sounding
  low-effort — it's part of the "flat / looks like AI slop" feeling you flagged.
- It applies to **every future video automatically**, at no extra cost per video.
- It's one shared step, so both niches (and any new ones later) are covered at once.

## How to check it works (click by click)
1. Start the app: `npm run go`.
2. Generate a **True Crime** or **History** video (run one of those factories).
3. Open it in the **Review Inbox** and play it:
   - The voice says **"F B I"** for FBI and reads years naturally.
   - The **on-screen captions still show "FBI"** and the original year digits —
     not the spelled-out version.
4. To add your own pronunciation later: add a **Setting** named
   `pronunciation_lexicon` with JSON like
   `{ "respell": { "gaddafi": "guh-DAH-fee" }, "acronyms": ["DA"] }`.
   Bad JSON is ignored safely, so a typo can never break narration.

## What I deliberately left out (kept the change small)
- The **optional "confirm this pronunciation?" prompt** in the Review Inbox for
  names the system doesn't recognise — a good fast-follow, but it needs new UI.
- **Multi-word** lexicon entries (e.g. "Ada Lovelace" as one phrase). Single-word
  names are supported now.
- A friendly **Settings screen** for the pronunciation list (today it's the JSON
  setting above). Also a good fast-follow.

## What could break
- **Low risk.** The pass is conservative and wrapped so that if anything ever goes
  wrong it silently falls back to the raw text — TTS never fails because of this.
- The only place captions could be affected is the Kokoro word-timing path; there
  the code re-checks its own work and, on any mismatch, falls back to the safe
  original-text captions rather than ever showing the spoken form.
- **Tested:** 47 new/updated unit tests; full suite (242 passing), lint, and
  production build all green.

## What's wrong

Your TikTok channel can silently go dark, and the app will keep telling you TikTok is "Connected."

We already fixed this exact problem for **YouTube** (you merged it — "Warn when your YouTube login expires"). When a YouTube login goes stale, the app flips it to **"Reconnect needed"** and shows a banner in Settings. **TikTok has none of that.**

Right now, when your TikTok login expires or gets revoked (TikTok refresh tokens expire on a fixed schedule, so this *will* happen), the code just throws an error deep in the publishing step and gives up. - `src/lib/tiktok.ts:164-169` — the app considers TikTok "connected" as long as a row is marked `active`; the throw above never changes it away from `active`.

## What to build

Mirror the YouTube reconnect flow for TikTok: when a TikTok token refresh fails because the session is dead, flip that connection's status to `needs_reconnect`, and show the same "Reconnect needed" banner for TikTok in Settings that YouTube already gets.

**M** — the YouTube version already exists as a template to copy.

## How we'd know it worked
Revoke/expire the TikTok login, run a publish, and Settings shows a "TikTok — reconnect needed" banner instead of a green "Connected," matching YouTube's behavior.

**S–M** — small change to two functions plus one surfacing hook.

title: Stop the sports/reddit channel mass-producing near-identical videos (#17)
body:
Closes #17

## What changed
Your True Crime and History channels already have a built-in brake that stops them publishing videos that look like the same template stamped out over and over. The **sports/reddit** channel did **not** have this — it would happily auto-publish near-duplicates back to back.

This PR gives the sports/reddit channel the same protection. Before a video is approved, it now quietly compares it against the last 15 videos from the **same** channel and checks two things:

- **Same opening again?** Is the title + hook almost word-for-word one you posted recently?
- **Same clip again?** Was it built from the exact same source highlight reel as a recent video?

If either is true, the video is **held for review instead of being auto-published**, and a plain-English reason shows up on the dashboard queue (in red) so you know why.

## Why it matters
YouTube's 2025–2026 crackdown demonetizes — and has terminated — channels whose uploads are repetitive and template-identical. This closes the biggest gap: the one channel that was mass-producing with no brake at all. It never blocks a video outright; it just parks the suspicious ones in your Review inbox so a wall of identical uploads never goes out on its own.

## How to check it works (click by click)
1. Start the app: `npm run go`, open http://localhost:3000
2. Run your sports agent a few times back-to-back on the **same** source (so it makes very similar videos).
3. Watch the Review inbox / dashboard:
   - The **first** video goes through as normal.
   - The **near-duplicate** ones land in **Review** instead of auto-publishing, and the queue shows a note like *"Built from the exact same source clip as a recent video…"* or *"Title/hook is 90% identical to a recent video…"*.
4. A genuinely different sports video still sails through untouched.

## What could break
- It only ever sends things to **Review** — it can never delete a video, block a good one hard, or stop a run. If it can't read the database for any reason, it simply passes the video through (fails safe).
- It's deliberately conservative: it compares only within the **same** channel, so a sports video is never compared against a true-crime one.
- If you ever *want* to reuse the same clip on purpose, the video isn't lost — it just waits for you in Review, one click to approve.

## Notes for a reviewer
- Reuses the existing similarity math (extracted `shingles`/`jaccard` into one shared file so the two gates can't drift) and the existing `resolveFinalStatus` used by the other pipelines — no new database tables, no schema migration.
- The decision logic is a pure function with unit tests (first-video passes, near-identical title flagged, same-clip flagged, empty scripts don't false-flag). Full suite: **234 passing**, production build green.

title: Some sports videos silently fail to render when the AI hook has a comma or % — fix the text escaping
body:
## What's wrong
Some sports videos fail to render for a reason that has nothing to do with the video — it's the wording of the on-screen hook text. If the AI writes a hook containing a **comma** or a **percent sign** (e.g. *"Down 3, ice in his veins"* or *"Shot 60% from three"*), the final render step crashes and the whole video is marked failed. It retries, but every retry fails identically because the text never changes.

## Why it matters
Curiosity-gap hooks routinely use commas — they're some of the best-performing openers. So this quietly kills a chunk of good videos before they're ever made, wasting the AI + footage cost that already went into them, and the owner just sees "failed" with a cryptic error.

## Evidence (this is a real, provable bug)
- `src/lib/tools/assemble.ts:57` escapes the hook with only: strip `\`, strip `'`, escape `:`. It does **not** handle `,` `%` `[` `]`. That text is then dropped into a comma-separated ffmpeg filter chain, so a comma inside the hook is read as a new filter and ffmpeg errors out.
- The codebase already has the correct fix sitting right next door: `src/lib/tools/transform.ts:60` (`escapeText`) strips `,` `[` `]` `%` properly. The sports assemble step just doesn't call it.

## Effort
**S** — reuse the existing `escapeText` helper in the sports assemble path.

## How we'd know it worked
A sports video whose hook contains a comma and a `%` renders successfully instead of failing, and a quick test feeding such a hook to the assemble step passes.

title: The dashboard's "$ cost" isn't real money — label it as an estimate and fix the blank sports figure
body:
## First — your question answered (no real money is being taken)

You asked: *"what money is being spent, what have I linked up account-wise, and where is the money being taken from?"* Straight answer:

- **Nothing is charged per video, and no payment account is linked inside this app.** There is no card, no bank, no Anthropic billing account wired into the platform. It can't take money from anywhere.
- The **"$" figures on the dashboard are estimates, not bills.** Every time the app calls Claude to write or narrate a video, it records how many words (tokens) that used, then multiplies by Anthropic's *public list price* to show "if you were paying per use, this is what it'd cost."
- Because you're on the **Claude Max 20× flat plan**, that usage is already covered by your monthly subscription. The estimate is a *yardstick to compare niches*, not money leaving your pocket.

So the honest fix here isn't just "make sports show a number" — it's **stop the number from looking like a live bill**, and make all niches consistent.

## What to build

Two small things, together:

1. **Label the figure honestly.** Rename the dashboard metric from a bare "$ cost" to something like **"Est. usage (at list price)"** with a one-line tooltip: *"Estimated token cost at Anthropic's public rates — covered by your Max plan, not a charge."* So you're never alarmed by it again.
2. **Fix the sports blank.** Sports videos currently show nothing at all, while true-crime and history show an estimate — an inconsistent, misleading gap. Roll the sports ledger rows up onto the video the same way the other niches already do, so every niche reports the same honest estimate.

## Why it matters

The spend tracker only earns its place if you trust it. Right now it does the opposite of building trust: it shows scary dollar signs that read like real charges, **and** it's blank for sports so you can't even compare niches. Fixing both turns it into what it was meant to be — a simple "which niche uses the most AI" gauge you can glance at without worry.

## Evidence

- The figures are **computed estimates, not charges**: `claudeCallCost()` multiplies token counts by list price (`src/lib/settings.ts:83-108`, comment: *"USD per input/output token"*). Nothing in the app connects to a payment provider.
- True-crime/history roll ledger rows into `Video.costEstimate` (`src/lib/truecrime/orchestrator.ts:295-304`); the **sports** orchestrator (`src/lib/orchestrator.ts`) has no equivalent step, so its `costEstimate` stays null.
- The dashboard only renders the figure when non-null (`inbox-card.tsx:222`, `page.tsx:486`) — hence sports shows blank — with no wording that says "estimate."

## Effort

**S–M** — the sports roll-up reuses the existing pattern (S); the honest re-label + tooltip is a small UI copy change (S).

## How we'd know it worked

A new sports video shows the same estimated figure the other niches do, **and** that figure is clearly labelled as an estimate covered by your plan — so glancing at the dashboard tells you which niche uses the most AI, with zero worry that money is being taken.

title: Stop TikTok from silently shadowbanning you — human-like posting + a 'your reach just died' alert
body:
## What to build
Two guardrails against TikTok quietly throttling the account for looking like a bot: (1) **humanized posting** — stagger posts on believable, slightly varied times instead of bulk/identical drops, and never cross-post a byte-identical file+caption to TikTok that already went to YouTube; (2) a **reach-drop alert** — if TikTok views suddenly collapse to near-zero across posts, warn the owner that he may be shadowbanned.

Shadowbans are the #1 TikTok creator complaint, and automated bulk posting + reused metadata + robotic TTS are exactly what triggers them. When it happens, reach silently drops to ~zero for **14-30 days** with **no notification** — the owner would keep posting into a void and never know. For a channel that isn't monetized yet, a month of dead reach is devastating.

## Evidence
- "Unoriginal content is a massive trigger for TikTok shadowbans… reduced reach to zero if the metadata matches an existing video." — https://later.com/blog/tiktok-shadowban/
- "Using third-party automation tools can make TikTok's system think you're a bot and trigger restrictions fast." Typical shadowban 14-30 days. — https://litcommerce.com/blog/tiktok-shadow-ban/

- This pairs with the TikTok-metrics work (needed to detect the reach drop) and the scheduler already exists (`src/lib/scheduler.ts`).

## Effort
**M** — add jitter/spacing to the scheduler for TikTok, ensure per-platform metadata differs, and flag sudden reach collapse.

## How we'd know it worked
TikTok posts go out on staggered, human-looking times with platform-specific captions, and if views crater across recent posts the owner gets a clear "possible shadowban — pause posting" warning.

title: Some true-crime/history videos get their narration cut off halfway — and still auto-publish
body:
## The problem in plain English

Some true-crime and history videos get their **narration cut off partway through** — the voice is telling the story and the video just ends early — and the app still treats them as finished and **auto-publishes them**. The owner never gets warned.

This happens on the most common footage path (the free Wikimedia still-image slideshow that true-crime and history videos fall back to when no video clips are available), so it is not a rare edge case.

## Why it happens (one specific spot)

In `src/lib/truecrime/assemble.ts` (used by BOTH true-crime and history), the app builds the picture track two ways:

- **The video-clip path** already protects itself: if any segment fails to render, it throws the whole thing away so the pictures always cover the full narration. There's even a comment explaining exactly this danger:
  > "A partial timeline (some segment failed to render) would sum to LESS than the narration, and the final `-shortest` mux would then cut the voice off mid-story." (`assemble.ts:212-216`)

- **The slideshow fallback path right below it does NOT have that protection** (`assemble.ts:220-226`). It renders each still image and only keeps the ones that succeed. If, say, 3 of 6 images fail to render (a corrupt download, a timeout), you get a picture track half the length of the narration. The final step stitches audio + picture with `-shortest` (`assemble.ts:280`), so the **finished video is cut to the short picture track — the second half of the story is gone.**

The final safety check (`isEmptyRender` in `src/lib/pipeline/finalize.ts:23`) only asks "does a video file exist?" — a half-length video answers yes, so it passes and gets marked approved/published. This is the exact failure the same file says it exists to prevent (it cites issue #14, "stop marking broken or silent videos as done").

## What to build

- In the slideshow fallback, apply the **same guard the video path already uses**: if not every still rendered, either stretch the survivors to cover the full audio duration or discard-and-fall-back — never ship a picture track shorter than the narration.
- Add a belt-and-braces **duration check** to the finalize gate: if the finished video is meaningfully shorter than the narration audio (e.g. >1s short), treat it as a broken render and hold for review instead of publishing.

## Evidence

- `src/lib/truecrime/assemble.ts:212-216` — the guard that protects the video path (and the comment naming this exact bug).
- `src/lib/truecrime/assemble.ts:220-226` — the slideshow path that is missing that guard.
- `src/lib/truecrime/assemble.ts:280` — the `-shortest` mux that does the truncating.
- `src/lib/pipeline/finalize.ts:23` — `isEmptyRender` only checks a file exists, not that it's complete.

## Effort
**S** — the fix mirrors a guard the codebase already has a few lines above, plus a short duration check in the finalize gate.

## How we'd know it worked
A test where some (but not all) slideshow stills fail to render no longer produces a published video shorter than its narration — it's held for review instead. In real runs, no true-crime/history video ends before its voiceover finishes.

title: Give YouTube and TikTok their own copy of each video, so they stop burying it as 'reused content'
body:
## What to build
When the app posts the same short to both YouTube Shorts and TikTok, it currently uploads the **same rendered file** to both. Platforms detect a re-used/downloaded file (by its embedded metadata fingerprint, and by any baked-in platform watermark) and quietly show it to far fewer people. We should give each platform its **own uniquely-encoded copy**: strip/refresh the file's metadata, make sure no foreign watermark is baked in, and re-encode a clean per-platform master before upload. A quick pre-publish check should also confirm the file we're about to post has no other platform's watermark on it.

## Why it matters
This is one of the most-cited reasons creators' cross-posts "flop." A widely-shared comparison: a watermarked TikTok re-posted to Shorts averaged **~450 views**, vs **~12,000 views** for a clean native master of the *same* video — a ~25x difference. YouTube itself says non-original-looking uploads get suppressed: *"Uploading content with visible watermarks signals to YouTube that this isn't original… even if it's your own content."* Because this app auto-publishes to **both** platforms, it's walking straight into this penalty on every video.

This is **not** the same as the existing "duplicate video" proposal (#71, which stops the *same* video going out *twice*) or the "blurry export" proposal (#76, which is about resolution/quality). This is about each platform seeing a distinct, clean, native-looking file.

## Evidence
- Watermark/metadata reach penalty: https://joyspace.ai/stop-reposting-tiktoks-watermark-detection
- YouTube reused-content policy: https://vidiq.com/blog/post/youtube-reused-content-policy-guide/
- Codebase: no metadata-stripping or per-platform re-encode exists — grep for \`map_metadata\`/\`watermark\` across \`src/\` returns nothing; both platforms are handed the same output path.

## Effort
**M** — a per-platform export step (ffmpeg metadata strip + light re-encode) plus a pre-publish watermark sanity check.

## How we'd know it worked
The same short posted to YouTube and TikTok arrives as two byte-different files with clean metadata and no foreign watermark, and cross-posted videos stop showing the tell-tale ~20x view gap versus a fresh upload.

Those videos can auto-publish and silently earn **$0**.

## Why it matters to the product's success
YouTube's "limited ads" state (the yellow dollar icon) zeroes out ad revenue on a video **even after your channel is monetized** — a 100% loss on views you were counting on. Two of the three factories are already protected from this; sports, one of your highest-volume factories, is not. Sports content is exactly where this bites: "hardest hits" / injury highlights and betting-odds overlays are staple sports-shorts formats, and YouTube **tightened its gambling-content rules in Nov 2025**, so betting-adjacent sports content is a live, current demonetization risk.

The good news: **the gate already exists in your code** — it just isn't wired to sports. So this is porting existing, tested logic to one more factory, not building something new.

- `src/lib/compliance/gate.ts:39` — `gateVideoScript` runs `evaluateCaseSelection`, which blocks/warns on gore and permanently-demonetized subject matter. True-crime and history both call this: `src/lib/truecrime/orchestrator.ts:2` and `src/lib/history/orchestrator.ts:12` (`import { gateVideoScript ... }`).
- `src/lib/compliance/caseSelection.ts:8-20` — the existing advertiser-friendly rules (permanent-demonetize list + gore heuristics), with a comment noting "gore is not advertiser-friendly on any topic."
- `src/lib/orchestrator.ts:8` — the **sports** orchestrator imports only `gateSportsCopyright` (a copyright gate). It never calls `gateVideoScript` / `evaluateCaseSelection`. There is **no** advertiser-friendly, injury, or gambling check anywhere in the sports path (confirmed: a repo-wide search for `advertiser`/`gambling`/`injury` outside `src/lib/compliance` returns nothing).

## Effort
**S–M** — reuse the existing `evaluateCaseSelection` pattern (or a small sports profile of it: injury/fight + gambling/betting terms) at the sports script/topic stage, and add a sports-specific term list. No new subsystem.

## How we'd know it worked

title: The crash-recovery safety net can wrongly kill a video that's still rendering — and make you pay to render it twice
body:
## What to build
Give the crash-recovery sweeper a safety margin so it can't kill a video that is *legitimately still rendering*. Right now the sweeper's "this run is dead, mark it failed" timeout is set to the **exact same 30 minutes** that a render is *allowed* to take — so a slow-but-healthy render can be declared "failed" at the very moment it's about to finish.

## Why it matters to the product's success
The recovery sweeper exists to rescue runs orphaned by a crash. But its cutoff and the render budget are identical:

- `src/lib/recovery.ts:19` — `DEFAULT_STUCK_TIMEOUT_MS = 30 * 60_000` (mark anything in flight >30 min as "failed").
- `src/lib/truecrime/orchestrator.ts:388` — `STAGE_TIMEOUT_MS = { assemble: 30 * 60_000 }` (a render is *allowed* 30 min; the code comment says assemble "gets extra headroom … incl. the one-time Chromium download"). The sports pipeline grants the same headroom (`src/lib/orchestrator.ts:241`).

With **zero margin** between "allowed to take 30 min" and "killed at 30 min," a genuine long render — plausible on the first Remotion render (one-time Chromium download) or a slower machine — gets swept to `failed` while ffmpeg/Remotion is still actively encoding. The video row only stamps its timestamp when rendering *starts* (`src/lib/recovery.ts:88-94` sweeps on `updatedAt`), so the sweeper can't tell "still working" from "actually dead."

Two harms:
1. The owner sees a **false "failed"** on a video that was about to succeed.
2. If he re-triggers it (the whole point of the "interrupted — re-run?" UX), he pays for a **second full render + TTS + image generation** on a video that would have finished on its own — real, avoidable spend.

This is distinct from proposal #102 (which *relies on* this same 30-min sweeper as its safety net for a hung sports fetch). This proposal fixes the sweeper itself so it doesn't misfire on healthy renders.

## Evidence (from this repo)
- `src/lib/recovery.ts:19` and `src/lib/truecrime/orchestrator.ts:388` — the two 30-minute values that must not be equal.
- `src/lib/recovery.ts:14-16` — the code's own comment admits a too-tight timeout causes a false-positive and hopes it "self-heals," which still surfaces a wrong "failed" and invites a double-spend re-run in the meantime.

## Effort
**S** — raise the recovery cutoff comfortably above the longest stage budget (e.g. 45–60 min), and/or "heartbeat" the video's `updatedAt` periodically during assemble so recovery can distinguish a live render from a dead one.

## How we'd know it worked
A test with a 29-minute-old `rendering` video (assemble budget 30 min) confirms the sweeper leaves it alone; a real ~25–30 min first render completes and publishes without ever flipping to "failed" mid-render.

title: Make the budget cap actually stop a run (#26)
body:
## What changed
The **"budget cap per run"** box on the New Agent screen used to do **nothing** — it was saved but never checked. The screen promised the run would "abort… if Claude + media costs exceed this amount," but no code ever read the cap, so a run could keep billing past your limit with no brake.

This makes the cap **real**. While a video is being made, the system now totals what the run has spent and **stops it the moment that total reaches your cap**, marking the run failed with a plain message: **"Stopped: run hit your $X budget cap."** That reason now shows on the **home/Overview screen** (the Queue tab already showed it). Works for all three video types — **sports, true crime, and history**.

Leave the cap **blank** (or set it to 0) and nothing changes — runs behave exactly as before.

## Why it matters
Every video spends real money (paid voice, image generation, Claude). A run stuck in a retry loop or an over-eager overnight batch could bill unbounded. You set a cap *specifically* so that couldn't happen, and the app told you it was handled — this closes that gap and keeps the promise the screen makes.

## How to check it works (click by click)
1. Go to **Agents** → **New Agent**.
2. In the **budget cap per run** box, type a tiny number: **0.001**. Save it.
3. Click **Run** on that agent.
4. Open the **home/Overview** screen (or the **Queue** tab). Within a step or two the run turns **Failed** with the red line **"Stopped: run hit your $0.001 budget cap."**
5. Now make another agent with the cap **left blank** and run it — it proceeds normally, proving nothing changed for uncapped agents.

## What could break
- **Small and contained:** 33 new lines across the three pipelines plus one shared helper, all behind the "is a cap set?" check — with no cap, there's not even a database read, so existing runs are untouched.
- **Honest limit:** the stop happens **between** steps, so the one step that crosses the line finishes before the run halts — real spend can land a touch over the cap, never far past it. Stopping mid-step would need up-front cost estimates and is out of scope here.
- New unit tests cover the cap logic (over/at/under the cap, blank/zero/negative = no cap, sub-cent caps like $0.001). Full test suite (480 tests), production build, and lint all pass.
